Confidentiality and the threat model

Source: vignettes/confidentiality.Rmd
confidentiality.Rmd

Why

A data owner about to send a synthetic table to a collaborator needs to know what it protects, what it does not, and what happens if a column’s sensitivity is set wrongly. This vignette covers all three, with examples that trigger the package’s safeguards.

masque gives no formal privacy guarantee such as differential privacy. It makes stand-in tables that keep the structure of an experiment, so analysis code can be written before the real data are used. Read this vignette before sharing any masque output beyond your own machine.

What

The recipe holds the real labels, the original column names and the seed. With the synthetic it undoes every alias, so keep it with the original data and never send it with the synthetic. The design assumes that only the synthetic crosses the trust boundary:

Actor holds Wants to learn What masque protects
Synthetic only Original raw values By default, every outcome and covariate value, replaced by independent draws. In the default and collaborate modes, treatment and categorical covariate labels replaced by codes, and ids and free text dropped. Categorical design labels are coded in the default mode, and in collaborate mode only a detected environment is. In collaborate mode, numerics are re-drawn from the observed distribution and jittered within a measurement step, so individual values may be near-exact copies, though not linked to their rows. Optionally, the column names
Synthetic + recipe Original raw values Nothing: together they undo every alias
Recipe only Original raw values The row values, which the recipe does not hold. It does hold the real labels, the original column names, the seed and each numeric column’s range
Synthetic + external side information Identity of treatments / sites Where labels are aliased or coded, the vocabulary and its order. A preserved design footprint or a keep column is recognisable, level frequencies are unchanged, and side information can often match them
Conditional clone (conditional = TRUE) Outcome mean of a treatment or design level Nothing: the clone reproduces the outcome mean of each treatment, block and environment level. A level with only a few plots reveals close to its real mean; a level with a single plot is pooled with the other single-plot levels first

masque keeps enough structure for a pipeline to run unchanged. Three modes set the balance between privacy and fidelity. Every translation is written to a private recipe, and a clone meant to be shared is audited when it is made.

It does not make output safe for public release. It does not hide rare strata, small designs, thin site-by-year cells or personal details in a column whose name does not give them away, and it does not change pipeline code.

Every column carries a role (what it is) and an action (how deeply it is masked: keep, noise, scramble, alias or drop). role_options() lists the pairs the package accepts. The mode argument of mask() chooses the defaults, so the common case needs no per-column work.

By default, every outcome and covariate is simulated independently. Each numeric column keeps only an eleven-point summary: its 1st percentile, deciles and 99th percentile. Only the experimental design and the pattern of missing values are kept exactly, and labels are replaced by codes. This is mode = "null". It keeps none of the relationships among outcome and covariate values. The design layout, the joint pattern of missing cells and which columns are constant within a unit remain visible.

If a pipeline needs those relationships, choose a mode that keeps them. mode = "local" is for the data owner’s own development and keeps labels as they are. mode = "collaborate" keeps the same structure for a clone shared with someone else, with labels aliased, numerics jittered and the audit run at mask time:

Knob mode = "null" (default) mode = "local" mode = "collaborate"
Design columns structure exact; categorical labels coded (<col>_D001), numeric columns kept kept kept; a categorical environment detected with high confidence is aliased
Treatment labels, numeric doses included aliased (trt_001) kept aliased (trt_001)
Categorical covariate labels drawn uniformly over the levels, coded (<col>_L001) kept aliased (<col>_L001)
Numeric outcomes and covariates drawn independently from a piecewise-linear curve through the 1st percentile, the deciles and the 99th percentile, so every draw lies between the 1st and 99th percentiles; whole numbers stay whole, and rounding can take one just outside; a column with fewer than 12 finite values takes the standard draw Gaussian copula with empirical-quantile marginals (may emit observed values) the same, plus within-resolution jitter, with whole numbers stochastically rounded. A value can fall up to half a measurement step outside the observed range, and a whole number up to one full step, so a column whose minimum is 0 can show -1. A conditional clone can go further, because it adds level effects after the draw
Date / time columns drawn independently within the approximate range, class preserved row-permuted with class preserved row-permuted with class preserved
Identifiers (id) dropped kept dropped
Free text (text: a character column in which more than half the values are distinct) dropped kept dropped
Columns constant within a design unit one independent draw per unit; the standard draw when fewer than 12 units are observed one value per unit, drawn from the real unit values one value per unit, jittered, or row by row when there are fewer than five units
NA mask preserved cell-by-cell preserved cell-by-cell preserved cell-by-cell
conditional = TRUE refused available available
audit_mask() automatic at mask() time on demand automatic at mask() time
handover() accepted refused unless allow_local = TRUE accepted
print(recipe) redacted; reveal_maps() shows the maps redacted; reveal_maps() shows the maps redacted; reveal_maps() shows the maps

Example

What a default clone keeps

A small trial with four sites, a site-level rainfall, a sowing date, a soil class and two missing yields shows each default action at work:

null_trial <- data.frame(
  site = factor(rep(c("Roseworthy", "Minnipa", "Turretfield", "Hart"),
                    each = 6L)),
  rep = rep(seq_len(3L), 8L),
  sown = as.Date("2021-05-01") + sample(0:30, 24L, replace = TRUE),
  soil = factor(sample(c("clay", "loam", "sand"), 24L, replace = TRUE)),
  rainfall = rep(c(300, 420, 510, 380), each = 6L),
  yield = round(rnorm(24L, 3, 0.5), 2),
  note = sprintf("plot note %d", seq_len(24L))
)
null_trial$yield[c(2L, 9L)] <- NA
plan_null <- propose_roles(null_trial, detect = FALSE)
knitr::kable(
  plan_null[, c("col", "role", "action")],
  caption = "The default masking plan."
)
The default masking plan.
col role action
site design alias
rep design keep
sown date noise
soil covariate noise
rainfall covariate noise
yield outcome noise
note text drop 
s_null <- synthetic(mask(null_trial, plan_null, seed = 1L))
#> Warning: rainfall has 4 observed units, fewer than 12. A summary of so few gives the values back,
#> so it was drawn as standard noise.
knitr::kable(
  head(s_null, 8L),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The first eight rows of the default clone."
)
The first eight rows of the default clone.
site rep sown soil rainfall yield
site_D003 1 2021-05-16 soil_L002 5 3.38
site_D003 2 2021-05-07 soil_L001 5 NA
site_D003 3 2021-05-10 soil_L003 5 3.34
site_D003 1 2021-05-02 soil_L001 5 2.92
site_D003 2 2021-05-27 soil_L003 5 2.89
site_D003 3 2021-05-23 soil_L002 5 2.95
site_D004 1 2021-05-03 soil_L001 4 2.95
site_D004 2 2021-05-26 soil_L002 4 3.34

The site labels are codes and each site keeps its six plots. soil is drawn uniformly over three coded levels. The sowing dates are drawn within the range of the real ones. Rainfall is constant within each site, so it gets one draw per site. Four sites are fewer than the twelve observed values a summary draw needs, so rainfall takes the standard draw and mask() warns. The free-text note is dropped. The missing yields stay in the same rows, and every drawn yield lies within the 1st and 99th percentiles of the real ones:

identical(is.na(s_null$yield), is.na(null_trial$yield))
#> [1] TRUE
tapply(s_null$rainfall, s_null$site, function(x) length(unique(x)))
#> site_D001 site_D002 site_D003 site_D004 
#>         1         1         1         1
range(s_null$yield, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 2.455462 3.583464
quantile(null_trial$yield, c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)
#>     1%    99% 
#> 2.3814 3.6527

noise = "standard" ignores the values and uses only each column’s type. A 0/1 column is drawn from Bernoulli(0.5), a proportion from Beta(2, 2), non-negative whole numbers from Poisson(5), other whole numbers from N(0, 5) rounded, other non-negative numbers from Gamma(2, 1), any other number from N(0, 1), and dates uniformly within the year 2000. Rainfall, recorded in whole millimetres, therefore comes out near 5:

s_std <- synthetic(
  mask(null_trial, plan_null, seed = 1L, noise = "standard")
)
knitr::kable(
  head(s_std[, c("site", "sown", "rainfall", "yield")], 4L),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The first rows of a clone drawn with `noise = \"standard\"`."
)
The first rows of a clone drawn with noise = "standard".
site sown rainfall yield
site_D002 2000-07-21 5 2.77
site_D002 2000-03-25 5 NA
site_D002 2000-05-13 5 1.10
site_D002 2000-01-24 5 1.26

Two columns with the same type flags draw the same values under one seed, whatever their means, because the flags are all a standard draw reads.

The summary is small, but it is not nothing. Three facts bound what it gives away. A column of eleven or fewer finite values can be read back exactly from its eleven points, which is why such a column takes the standard draw. Below 101 values the 1st percentile is interpolated from the minimum, so the minimum enters the summary, and the maximum enters it the same way through the 99th percentile. And many clones of one table, each drawn under a different seed, estimate the eleven points ever more closely. A clone should therefore be made once and shared once, as for a second jitter of the same table: a second draw under a new seed adds nothing for the developer and narrows the estimate for anyone holding both.

Hiding design labels

The default mode already codes categorical design labels. In local and collaborate mode design columns are byte-identical, apart from a detected environment in collaborate mode, which preserves the experimental layout exactly, labels included. A publicly registered trial layout is a fingerprint. To keep the structure but hide the site or block labels in those modes, set a design column’s action to alias:

df <- data.frame(
  site = factor(rep(c("Roseworthy", "Minnipa", "Turretfield"), each = 6L)),
  rep = rep(seq_len(3L), 6L),
  yield = rnorm(18L)
)
plan <- propose_roles(df, mode = "collaborate", detect = FALSE)
plan <- set_role(plan, "site", role = "design", action = "alias")
s <- synthetic(mask(df, plan, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L))
site_names_gone <- !any(as.character(s$site) %in% as.character(df$site))
site_names_gone
#> [1] TRUE
knitr::kable(
  as.data.frame(table(s$site), stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  col.names = c("aliased site", "plots"),
  caption = "The three-site structure survives even though the labels do not."
)
The three-site structure survives even though the labels do not.
aliased site plots
site_D001 6
site_D002 6
site_D003 6

Aliasing a design column breaks byte-identity, so local mode never does it by default, and collaborate mode does it only for a detected environment. Names can be hidden the same way: mask(..., alias_names = TRUE) replaces every retained column name with an opaque code that the recipe inverts on the round-trip, and alias_names = c("site", "yield") hides only those names.

What an alias does and does not hide. The alias vocabulary is fixed and sorted (trt_001, trt_002, …), but which level receives which alias is drawn from a random permutation, so for a six-level column there are 720 equally likely maps. This matters because the vocabularies in field research are routinely public: a variety roster, an N-rate ladder, a site list. The same draw governs the join keys mask_set() shares across tables.

Two limits remain, both for the data owner to manage:

  • The seed is confidential material. The permutation comes from the seeded stream, so the same call with the same seed reproduces the same map, exactly as it reproduces the same synthetic values. Publishing the seed beside the synthetic lets anyone who can rerun the call recover the map. Keep the seed with the recipe, or pass seed = NULL where reproducibility is not required and take a fresh map each call.
  • Frequencies are not hidden. Aliasing is a bijection on labels: the count of each level is unchanged by design, because the design footprint is what makes the clone useful. A vocabulary whose level counts are known and distinct is still matchable one level at a time. audit_mask() reports each column’s number of levels and its smallest level count.

An alias therefore raises the cost of re-identification. It cannot be relied on against a determined attacker, and none of it is a differential-privacy guarantee.

Numeric treatments

A dose or a nitrogen rate is a numeric treatment. Its values are often the most recognisable part of a trial, so the default and collaborate modes alias them, as they do treatment labels. The clone carries trt_001, trt_002, … as text, and the recipe turns them back into the exact numbers:

rates <- data.frame(
  block = factor(rep(seq_len(4L), each = 5L)),
  nitro = rep(c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8), 4L)
)
rates$yield <- round(80 + 40 * rates$nitro + rnorm(20L, sd = 5), 1)
plan_rates <- propose_roles(rates, mode = "collaborate")
m_rates <- mask(rates, plan_rates, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L)
knitr::kable(
  head(synthetic(m_rates), 5L),
  digits = 1,
  caption = "The first block of the clone: each N rate is an opaque label."
)
The first block of the clone: each N rate is an opaque label.
block nitro yield
1 trt_002 85.9
1 trt_005 93.2
1 trt_003 99.1
1 trt_004 113.2
1 trt_001 84.5 
identical(unmask(synthetic(m_rates), recipe(m_rates))$nitro, rates$nitro)
#> [1] TRUE

Every block still holds each rate once, so the design is intact. With action = "scramble" the rates stay numbers and are permuted among themselves instead. A numeric treatment left at keep or scramble in the default or collaborate mode audits HIGH, because every real rate stays visible.

The conditional clone: mimicking the treatment effect

In local and collaborate mode, numeric synthesis re-simulates every scrambled numeric column from one Gaussian copula with empirical-quantile marginals, fitted on the whole table. That preserves each column’s marginal distribution and, approximately, the global correlation, which is enough to develop most pipelines. It does not keep the relationship between treatment and outcome. The synthetic outcomes are drawn from the pooled distribution and the treatment labels are relabelled independently, so a model fitted on the clone sees no association between an arm and its response. A pipeline whose whole purpose is to estimate a treatment effect would silently give the wrong answer on such a clone.

mask()’s conditional = TRUE argument fixes this. It fits and samples the copula within each treatment-by-design stratum rather than pooling, so a row’s synthetic outcome inherits the location of the treatment that row carries. The treatment effect a model estimates is reproduced within sampling tolerance. A default clone keeps no treatment effect by design, so mask() refuses conditional = TRUE there and asks for mode = "local" or mode = "collaborate".

The contrast is easiest to see on a two-arm trial with a known effect:

set.seed(42)
n <- 600L
arm <- factor(rep(c("ctrl", "treat"), each = n / 2L))
# A real +5-unit effect of the treated arm on yield.
yield <- 10 + 5 * (arm == "treat") + rnorm(n, sd = 2)
trial <- data.frame(genotype = arm, yield = yield)

plan <- propose_roles(trial, mode = "local", detect = FALSE)
plan <- set_role(plan, "genotype", role = "treatment", action = "scramble")
plan <- set_role(plan, "yield", role = "outcome")

true_effect <- coef(lm(yield ~ genotype, trial))[["genotypetreat"]]
true_effect
#> [1] 4.988538

The next chunk clones the trial both ways from the same seed and re-estimates the effect on each clone:

marg <- mask(trial, plan, mode = "local", seed = 1L, conditional = FALSE)
cond <- mask(trial, plan, mode = "local", seed = 1L, conditional = TRUE)

effect_of <- function(m) {
  coef(lm(yield ~ genotype, synthetic(m)))[["genotypetreat"]]
}
effect_marg <- effect_of(marg)
effect_cond <- effect_of(cond)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    clone = c("marginal", "conditional"),
    estimated_effect = c(effect_marg, effect_cond),
    true_effect = true_effect
  ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = paste0(
    "The treated-arm effect, re-estimated on each clone against the ",
    "true effect fitted on the original trial."
  )
)
The treated-arm effect, re-estimated on each clone against the true effect fitted on the original trial.
clone estimated_effect true_effect
marginal 0.249 4.989
conditional 5.138 4.989

The marginal clone collapses the effect toward zero. The conditional clone recovers it. Both clones still match the pooled marginal of the outcome:

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    source = c("original", "marginal clone", "conditional clone"),
    mean_yield = c(
      mean(trial$yield), mean(synthetic(marg)$yield),
      mean(synthetic(cond)$yield)
    ),
    sd_yield = c(
      sd(trial$yield), sd(synthetic(marg)$yield),
      sd(synthetic(cond)$yield)
    )
  ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = paste0(
    "Both clones preserve the pooled mean and SD of yield; only the ",
    "conditional clone preserves the arm-to-arm difference."
  )
)
Both clones preserve the pooled mean and SD of yield; only the conditional clone preserves the arm-to-arm difference.
source mean_yield sd_yield
original 12.451 3.183
marginal clone 12.496 3.083
conditional clone 12.497 3.199

Figure: the effect on each clone 

effect_df <- data.frame(
  clone = factor(
    c("marginal", "conditional"),
    levels = c("marginal", "conditional")
  ),
  estimated_effect = c(effect_marg, effect_cond)
)
ggplot2::ggplot(
  effect_df, ggplot2::aes(x = clone, y = estimated_effect, fill = clone)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = true_effect, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "clone", y = "estimated treatment effect (yield units)"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

Estimated treatment effect (yield units) on the marginal versus conditional clone, against the true effect fitted on the original trial (dashed line). The marginal clone collapses the effect toward zero; the conditional clone recovers it.

The conditioning columns (the treatment plus any retained design columns) are recorded on the recipe, so the choice is auditable:

recipe(cond)@conditional
#> [1] TRUE
recipe(cond)@conditioning_cols
#> [1] "genotype"
recipe(cond)@conditioning_used
#> [1] "genotype"
recipe(cond)@fallback_frac
#> [1] 0

conditioning_cols is what the call asked for, conditioning_used is the stratum the clone got, and fallback_frac is the share of rows pooled into the fallback stratum. They can differ, because a conditional clone needs enough rows per stratum to fit a stratum-local copula, and the finest stratum available is rarely the one that has them. On a replicated factorial of six N rates by three varieties by four replicates, treatment crossed with every retained design column is seventy-two cells of one row. mask() therefore walks a coarsening ladder: it drops design columns until the cells hold at least five rows. Treatment columns are never dropped. Rows still in cells that are too small at the last rung are pooled into one fallback stratum.

The default ladder (ladder = "hierarchy") drops plot row and column positions first, then blocking columns, then environment columns, so a site is never given up before the replicates inside it. It carries the main effect of every dropped column into the clone as an additive shift. The site, replicate and block means of the original therefore survive even when the copula is fitted within the treatment alone. The threat table above lists what that discloses. The recipe lists the shifted terms as conditioning_shifted. ladder = "levels" reproduces clones made with masque 0.11.1 to 0.12.0: it drops the column with the most levels first and keeps nothing of it.

Any coarsening, and any residual pooling, raises a classed masque_conditional_degraded warning naming the columns given up and the pooled share, and both facts are written onto the recipe. A pipeline can catch the class if it should stop when its clone is less conditional than it asked for:

withCallingHandlers(
  mask(trial, plan, mode = "local", seed = 1L, conditional = TRUE),
  masque_conditional_degraded = function(w) stop(conditionMessage(w))
)

Conditional cloning works in local and collaborate mode and with mask_set(), where each table is stratified by its own treatment and design columns. With no treatment or design column to condition on at all, the clone falls back to the global copula and raises the same classed warning. Use it when the pipeline estimates an effect and you accept that it discloses each level’s outcome mean.

What the copula keeps: monotone association only

In local and collaborate mode, numeric columns that are re-simulated together share one Gaussian copula, fitted on the normal scores of their ranks. A Gaussian copula holds a single correlation per pair, so it reproduces a monotone association (linear, or any order-preserving curve) but not a dependence that a correlation cannot express. A non-monotone relationship, such as a U-shaped dependence of an outcome on a covariate, reads as near-zero rank correlation and is reproduced as near-independence.

set.seed(7)
n <- 2000L
x_lin <- rnorm(n)
y_lin <- 2 * x_lin + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)     # monotone (linear)
x_u <- runif(n, -3, 3)
y_u <- x_u^2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)           # non-monotone (U-shaped)
d <- data.frame(x_lin, y_lin, x_u, y_u)

s <- synthetic(mask(d, propose_roles(d, mode = "local", detect = FALSE),
                    mode = "local", seed = 1L))

# R-squared of a quadratic fit captures a linear or a U-shaped association.
fit_r2 <- function(x, y) summary(lm(y ~ poly(x, 2)))$r.squared
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    pair = c("monotone (y = 2x)", "non-monotone (y = x^2)"),
    original = c(fit_r2(x_lin, y_lin), fit_r2(x_u, y_u)),
    clone = c(fit_r2(s$x_lin, s$y_lin), fit_r2(s$x_u, s$y_u))
  ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = paste0(
    "R-squared of a quadratic fit, original versus clone, for a ",
    "monotone and a non-monotone pair."
  )
)
R-squared of a quadratic fit, original versus clone, for a monotone and a non-monotone pair.
pair original clone
monotone (y = 2x) 0.942 0.941
non-monotone (y = x^2) 0.966 0.000

The monotone pair keeps its association almost exactly. The non-monotone pair loses it entirely, so on the clone the covariate carries no information about the outcome. conditional = TRUE does not repair this: it preserves the outcome’s location within each treatment-by-design stratum, not the curvature of the outcome’s dependence on a continuous covariate. A pipeline whose modelling step is non-linear (a smoothing spline, a generalised additive model, a tree, an interaction term) sees on the synthetic only the monotone part of any relationship in the original. A good fit there is not evidence that the step behaves correctly on the real data. Validate such a step by running it on the original through the recipe.

Columns constant within a trial: the grain

Some columns describe a whole unit rather than a row: the rainfall of a trial, the soil type of a site, a sowing date. Re-simulated row by row, such a column would vary inside the trial, which no real trial does. mask() finds the design unit within which a column holds a single value and synthesises the column once per unit, writing each unit’s new value to all its rows. That unit is the column’s grain:

set.seed(3)
trials <- data.frame(
  trial = factor(rep(sprintf("T%d", seq_len(8L)), each = 12L)),
  rep = factor(rep(rep(seq_len(3L), each = 4L), 8L)),
  gen = factor(rep(sprintf("G%d", seq_len(4L)), 24L))
)
trial_rain <- round(runif(8L, 250, 550))
trials$rainfall <- trial_rain[as.integer(trials$trial)]
trials$yield <- round(2 + trials$rainfall / 200 + rnorm(96L, sd = 0.4), 2)

plan_trials <- propose_roles(trials, mode = "collaborate")
by_unit <- mask(trials, plan_trials, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L)
by_row <- mask(trials, plan_trials, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L,
               grain = FALSE)
values_per_trial <- function(m) {
  s <- synthetic(m)
  as.vector(tapply(s$rainfall, s$trial, function(x) length(unique(x))))
}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    clone = c("grain = TRUE (default)", "grain = FALSE"),
    distinct_rainfall_per_trial = c(
      paste(values_per_trial(by_unit), collapse = " "),
      paste(values_per_trial(by_row), collapse = " ")
    )
  ),
  caption = "Distinct rainfall values in each of the eight trials of the clone."
)
Distinct rainfall values in each of the eight trials of the clone.
clone distinct_rainfall_per_trial
grain = TRUE (default) 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1
grain = FALSE 7 6 7 5 10 9 8 7

propose_roles() notes such a column (“Constant within trial; synthesised per trial”), and the recipe records each grain. The clone keeps one value per unit. In local and collaborate mode it also keeps the frequencies of a categorical column across units and the correlation among columns of the same grain. It does not keep the correlation between a grained column and the row-level columns, so the link between rainfall and yield above is lost. Grained columns are not conditioned on treatment when conditional = TRUE.

In the default mode each unit gets one independent draw. In local mode the unit values are drawn from the real unit values. In collaborate mode they are jittered, and a grain with fewer than five units is synthesised row by row instead, with a masque_grain_small_units warning, because resampling so few real values would disclose them. The audit then notes that the clone does not keep that grain. grain = FALSE synthesises every column row by row.

Time-to-event outcomes

A clinical table often holds several event times on one row, such as time to recurrence and time to death, each with a status. Re-simulated as independent columns, the times would fall out of order. Declaring them to events keeps them linked. List the times in the order the events occur:

set.seed(5)
n_pat <- 300L
arm <- rep(c("A", "B"), length.out = n_pat)
t_rec <- rexp(n_pat, ifelse(arm == "A", 1 / 900, 1 / 1400))
t_death <- rexp(n_pat, 1 / 2500)
censor <- runif(n_pat, 30, 3000)
status_death <- as.integer(t_death <= censor)
time_death <- round(pmin(t_death, censor))
status_rec <- as.integer(t_rec < pmin(t_death, censor))
time_rec <- ifelse(status_rec == 1L, pmin(round(t_rec), time_death),
                   time_death)
patients <- data.frame(arm, time_rec, status_rec, time_death, status_death)

plan_pat <- propose_roles(patients, mode = "collaborate", detect = FALSE)
plan_pat <- set_role(plan_pat, "arm", role = "treatment")
for (cn in c("time_rec", "status_rec", "time_death", "status_death")) {
  plan_pat <- set_role(plan_pat, cn, role = "outcome", action = "scramble")
}
m_pat <- mask(
  patients, plan_pat, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L,
  events = list(time = c("time_rec", "time_death"),
                status = c("status_rec", "status_death"))
)
s_pat <- synthetic(m_pat)
all(s_pat$time_rec <= s_pat$time_death)
#> [1] TRUE
pattern <- function(d) paste(d$status_rec, d$status_death, sep = "/")
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    pattern = names(table(pattern(patients))),
    original = as.vector(table(pattern(patients))),
    clone = as.vector(table(pattern(s_pat)))
  ),
  caption = "Rows in each recurrence/death status pattern."
)
Rows in each recurrence/death status pattern.
pattern original clone
0/0 77 77
0/1 82 82
1/0 93 93
1/1 48 48

Within each status pattern the gaps between events are re-simulated and summed back into times. The times stay in order, a patient without a recurrence keeps both times equal, and the count of each pattern is exact. No final time runs past the longest follow-up observed in its pattern. The status patterns are permuted across rows, within each arm when conditional = TRUE, so a row’s pattern is no longer tied to the patient on that row, except by chance. No hazard model is fitted, and the clone keeps no relation between a covariate and the events.

The leakage audit, and a refused write

audit_mask() inspects the synthetic against the original and grades the leakage of each column. In the default and collaborate modes it runs automatically and warns at mask() time. The fixture below is built to trip it: a PII-suspected column kept against the default, and a categorical covariate with a frequency-one level.

df <- data.frame(
  rep = rep(seq_len(3L), each = 20L),
  variety = factor(rep(paste0("V", seq_len(6L)), 10L)),
  contact_email = factor(rep(c("a@x", "b@y"), 30L)),
  rare_treatment = factor(c(
    "only_one",
    sample(c("alpha", "beta", "gamma"), 59L, replace = TRUE)
  )),
  yield = rnorm(60L, 5, 1),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

plan <- propose_roles(df, mode = "collaborate")
knitr::kable(
  plan[, c("col", "role", "action", "pii_suspected")],
  caption = paste0(
    "The proposed plan: `contact_email` is auto-flagged ",
    "`pii_suspected` and dropped."
  )
)
The proposed plan: contact_email is auto-flagged pii_suspected and dropped.
col role action pii_suspected
rep design keep FALSE
variety treatment alias FALSE
contact_email text drop TRUE
rare_treatment treatment alias FALSE
yield outcome scramble FALSE

Suppose the data owner overrides the flag, keeps contact_email, and makes the rare column a covariate:

plan <- set_role(plan, "contact_email", role = "covariate", action = "keep")
plan <- set_role(plan, "rare_treatment", role = "covariate")
m <- mask(df, plan, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L)
#> Warning: audit_mask() flagged HIGH leakage on columns: contact_email, rare_treatment
knitr::kable(
  audit_mask(m, print = FALSE)[, c("col", "leakage_class", "notes")],
  caption = paste0(
    "The mask-time audit: `contact_email` and `rare_treatment` both ",
    "flag HIGH."
  )
)
The mask-time audit: contact_email and rare_treatment both flag HIGH.
col leakage_class notes
rep low exact-match 100.0%
variety low levels aliased
contact_email high PII-pattern column name; kept as-is - visible to collaborators; same-row 100.0% vs chance 50.0%
rare_treatment high levels aliased; rare level (freq = 1)
yield low ok

contact_email (real values kept across the trust boundary) and rare_treatment (a frequency-one level) are flagged. mask() raised a classed masque_high_leakage warning above and recorded the findings in recipe(m)@warnings. The guided masque() flow never silences it. While a HIGH finding stands, the package will not write the synthetic to disk:

out_dir <- tempfile()
masque(df, roles = plan, out = out_dir, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L,
       quiet = TRUE)
#> Warning: audit_mask() flagged HIGH leakage on columns: contact_email, rare_treatment
#> Error in `.gate_release()`:
#> ! Write blocked: the audit flagged HIGH leakage on 2 findings.
#> ✖ Flagged: contact_email, rare_treatment.
#> ℹ Re-role, alias, or drop each flagged column, then mask again.
#> ℹ Or pass `allow_high = TRUE` to write anyway after your own review - the override is recorded on
#>   the recipe.
dir.exists(out_dir)
#> [1] FALSE

Nothing is written. The two flagged columns are named in the message, and the remedy is spelled out (re-role, alias, or drop the column, then mask again). A data owner who has reviewed the findings and still wants to proceed can pass allow_high = TRUE. The override is itself raised as a classed masque_high_override warning and recorded in the recipe’s warnings, so the exception stays on record.

Each column is also graded on how far its row-by-row match with the original exceeds what chance gives. attr(audit_mask(m, print = FALSE), "joint") holds the table-level checks: rows whose every re-simulated column equals the original, and rare combinations of retained values. A HIGH table-level finding blocks the writers as a column finding does.

An outcome left at keep in the default or collaborate mode hands over the real responses, so it audits HIGH:

trial_kept <- data.frame(
  block = factor(rep(seq_len(4L), each = 6L)),
  variety = factor(rep(sprintf("V%d", seq_len(6L)), 4L)),
  height = round(rnorm(24L, 90, 8)),
  yield = round(rnorm(24L, 5, 1), 2)
)
plan_kept <- propose_roles(trial_kept, mode = "collaborate")
plan_kept <- set_role(plan_kept, "yield", role = "outcome", action = "keep")
m_kept <- mask(trial_kept, plan_kept, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L)
#> Warning: audit_mask() flagged HIGH leakage on column: yield
knitr::kable(
  audit_mask(m_kept, print = FALSE)[col == "yield", c("col", "leakage_class")],
  caption = "A kept outcome in a collaborate clone."
)
A kept outcome in a collaborate clone.
col leakage_class
yield high

If the data owner has decided the real outcome may be shared, passing allow_kept_outcome = TRUE grades the column medium and records the choice on the recipe:

m_allowed <- mask(trial_kept, plan_kept, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L,
                  allow_kept_outcome = TRUE)
knitr::kable(
  audit_mask(m_allowed, print = FALSE)[
    col == "yield", c("col", "leakage_class")
  ],
  caption = "The same outcome, allowed by the data owner."
)
The same outcome, allowed by the data owner.
col leakage_class
yield medium 
recipe(m_allowed)@allow_kept_outcome
#> [1] TRUE

The table-level checks still apply. When the kept outcome is the only column that would otherwise be re-simulated, the clone matches the original row for row, the whole-row check stays HIGH, and the writers stay blocked.

Small tables

Re-simulating a column of a few rows returns the original values in a new order, and a summary of a few values lies close to the values themselves. The default and collaborate modes therefore refuse a table of fewer than five rows when a column would be scrambled, or drawn as numeric or date noise:

tiny <- trial_kept[1:4, c("block", "yield")]
mask(tiny, propose_roles(tiny, mode = "collaborate"), mode = "collaborate",
     seed = 1L)
#> Error in `.check_row_floor()`:
#> ! `df` has 4 rows, fewer than 5, and yield would be re-simulated.
#> ✖ A re-simulated column this short is the original values resampled, so a clone meant to be shared
#>   would disclose them.
#> ℹ Keep, alias or drop that column, or mask a table of at least 5 rows.

Local mode warns instead. Kept, aliased and dropped columns are not re-simulated, and factor and character noise draws codes only, so a short lookup table of site codes masks in any mode. A logical noise column counts towards the floor, because it is drawn over the values it holds. Five rows is a floor, not a guarantee. A column of a few dozen rows still carries values close to the real ones, and jitter within a measurement step does little to hide them. The same applies to small strata of a conditional clone, which is why its cells hold at least five rows.

Beyond that gate the release decision stays with the data owner. Whether a synthetic table is appropriate for a given collaborator, environment, or jurisdiction depends on context the package cannot see. masque informs that decision. It does not make it.

Multi-table sets

When several tables share a key, mask_set() aliases that key identically across all of them so the synthetic tables still join. Permuting the key separately in each table would break the join.

set_dir <- system.file("extdata", "met_set", package = "masque")
tabs <- read_set(set_dir)
tabs$agronomy[, year := factor(year)]
ms <- mask_set(tabs, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L, quiet = TRUE)
ag <- synthetic(ms)$agronomy
qa <- synthetic(ms)$quality
join_survives <- setequal(unique(ag$gen), unique(qa$gen))
join_survives
#> [1] TRUE
head(unique(ag$gen), 3L)
#> [1] "gen_K056" "gen_K048" "gen_K017"

year is converted to a factor first. As a number it would be kept with its real values, with a warning, because masque does not propose aliasing for a numeric environment column. A linked key gets aliases of the form <col>_K001, such as gen_K001, from one map shared by every table.

The recipe bundle is private exactly as a single recipe is, and write_set() never writes it. save_recipe() and read_recipe() keep it as one .rds file, audit_mask(ms) returns one audit per table, and reveal_maps(recipe(ms), table = "agronomy") reveals the maps of one table.

Geographic coordinates

Latitude and longitude are treated as sensitive: propose_roles() flags a column whose name looks like a coordinate (gps, lat/latitude, lon/longitude) as pii_suspected and proposes drop. Dropping is the safest choice when the synthetic does not need locations.

A coordinate is masked unless told otherwise. If a column with a coordinate-like name is left at keep, mask() stops. There are three ways to say what happens to it:

  1. Declare the pair to coords, which displaces it.
  2. Give the column drop, noise or scramble, which masks it.
  3. Pass allow_unmasked_coords = TRUE after deciding the position is not sensitive. The recipe records this, so the decision is visible later.

A column that looks like a coordinate only by the shape of its values raises a warning instead of stopping, because that detection is a guess and a false positive should not block a legitimate mask.

When the synthetic does need plausible coordinates, to exercise a spatial pipeline say, a plain scramble or noise draw is the wrong tool: each axis is drawn on its own, which smears a latitude/longitude pair into a continuous cloud that can land in the sea. masque offers two purpose-built alternatives.

jitter_coordinates() displaces coordinates in place by a geographic-masking jitter. The default donut scheme displaces every site by a random distance drawn uniformly by area from an annulus, in a random direction, and re-draws until the point falls on land, so a coastal site is never pushed offshore. The longitude step is corrected by cos(latitude) so the ground distance matches the requested kilometres at any latitude, and the NA pattern and the latitude/longitude pairing are preserved.

sites <- data.frame(
  site = c("A", "B", "C"),
  lat  = c(-34.9, -35.2, -33.6),
  lon  = c(138.6, 142.0, 148.2)
)
knitr::kable(
  jitter_coordinates(sites, "lat", "lon", min_km = 5, max_km = 20, seed = 1L),
  digits = 4,
  caption = paste0(
    "Three sites, each displaced 5-20 km in a random direction and ",
    "re-drawn until on land."
  )
)
Three sites, each displaced 5-20 km in a random direction and re-drawn until on land.
site lat lon
A -34.7837 138.6072
B -35.2466 141.8980
C -33.7258 148.1070

A coordinate belongs to a site, not to a row. One displacement is drawn per site and applied to every row of that site, so a table holding many rows per physical place (plots within a trial, samples within a paddock) comes back with one masked coordinate per place, exactly as the source table has one true coordinate per place. By default a site is a set of rows sharing an identical input coordinate, which needs no user action and cannot alter genuinely point-level data. Where a site’s recorded coordinates differ slightly between rows, passing the site columns to by consolidates the group to its centroid.

plots <- data.frame(
  trial = rep(c("T1", "T2"), each = 4L),
  lat   = rep(c(-34.9, -35.2), each = 4L) + c(0, 1e-4, 2e-4, 3e-4),
  lon   = rep(c(138.6, 142.0), each = 4L)
)
masked <- jitter_coordinates(plots, "lat", "lon", by = "trial", seed = 1L)
#> Warning: 2 sites named by `by` hold more than one input coordinate and were consolidated to the site
#> centroid.
#> ℹ Sites: "T1" and "T2".
#> ℹ Widest internal spread 0 km.
one_coord_per_trial <- nrow(unique(masked[c("lat", "lon")])) == 2L
one_coord_per_trial
#> [1] TRUE

Grouping is a confidentiality control, not only a fidelity one. Donut displacement is isotropic, so the mean of many independent draws around one true site converges on that site. Displacing a 360-row trial row by row leaves its centroid a median 0.64 km from the truth, against the 5 km floor the donut was asked for. One draw per site removes that estimator and leaves the full displacement in place. The unit has to be chosen carefully: it is the finest grouping denoting one physical place at one time, so for a multi-year trial series it is location by year rather than location alone, because trials at one named location in different seasons legitimately sit in different paddocks. Each year at the same farm is then a separate draw, and averaging them narrows the area, so a long series at one farm needs a wider donut or one unit per farm.

A site that cannot be placed on land within max_tries re-draws is set to NA on both axes, with a warning. masque does not emit a true coordinate inside a table the caller believes is masked.

Declaring the pair to mask() applies the same displacement as part of masking, so the coordinates never pass through the copula. For a table with coordinate columns GPS_S and GPS_E and a TRIAL column, the call looks like this:

plan <- set_role(plan, c("GPS_S", "GPS_E"), action = "keep")
m <- mask(df, plan, mode = "collaborate",
          coords = list(list(lat = "GPS_S", lon = "GPS_E", by = "TRIAL")),
          seed = 1L)

The recipe records the grouping each declared pair was masked under, so the recipe records the site grouping used for each declared pair. A coordinate declared to coords is retained in the synthetic, so audit_mask() reports it as medium, noting that the column was displaced in place. A coordinate kept with its real values would be HIGH.

synthesise_geospatial() instead re-anchors points around fake centroids you supply for each region.

How far to displace. The right magnitude is not a constant. It is calibrated to the density of the entities being protected, so that the masked point is spatially k-anonymous: roughly, at least k comparable entities lie closer to the masked point than the true one (Hampton et al., 2010). Individual-level urban health data are typically masked by displacements of the order of a kilometre, because cities are dense (Zandbergen, 2014). Fields and farms are far sparser, so comparable protection needs a much larger displacement. The default donut of 5 to 20 km is chosen to move a point across several properties while keeping it in the same agroclimatic region. A stated k needs the radii calibrated to the local density of farms.

Results

Aliasing a design column hides the site names and keeps the layout. The alias map hides which label is which, but not how often each occurs.

A default clone keeps the experimental design, the missing cells and each column’s approximate range, and none of the relationships among the outcome and covariate values.

The marginal clone keeps the pooled mean and SD of yield but loses the treatment effect (0.25 against a true 4.99), and a pipeline that checks only marginal fidelity would not notice. The conditional clone keeps it (5.14). Neither keeps a non-monotone relationship between two numeric columns.

A column constant within a trial stays constant within it, and linked event times stay in order with exact pattern counts.

The audit caught both planted problems and the write was refused: dir.exists(out_dir) is FALSE. A kept outcome audits HIGH unless the data owner allows it, and a default or collaborate table of fewer than five rows is refused when a column would be resampled. Linked tables share one alias map for their key, so they still join.

A default or collaborate clone therefore replaces treatment and covariate labels and re-draws the values. It does not hide the design footprint or the frequencies of design and treatment levels, and without conditional = TRUE it does not keep a treatment effect. The audit flags the wrongly set columns it can see, such as a kept contact column, before anything is written.

Limits

Everything demonstrated here is a development safeguard, not a disclosure-control guarantee in the formal sense. The alias map raises the cost of a public-vocabulary attack, but a bijection preserves level frequencies. A determined attacker with strong side information about frequencies and structure is not stopped by an alias alone. The Gaussian copula of local and collaborate mode keeps only monotone association, so a pipeline whose core modelling step is non-linear should be validated on the original data through the recipe. The donut jitter’s k-anonymity property is a rule of thumb tied to entity density, not a certified guarantee, and the radius for a given dataset should be chosen with that density in mind. The leakage audit reads what the mask-time comparison can see (flagged names, frequency-one levels, retained coordinates). It cannot detect a disclosure risk that depends on information outside the table, such as an outside dataset an attacker might already hold.

What to read next

Getting started with masque covers the data owner’s side of a first masking run: masque(), the default clone and how to opt into structure, the roles-and-actions plan, and multi-environment detection. Recipe anatomy and the round-trip covers the return leg: what the recipe stores and how the data owner runs the finished pipeline on the original with it.

Reproduce

set.seed(1) is set once for the whole document and drives the default-clone, design-label and N-rate fixtures. The later leaky-audit and kept-outcome fixtures draw from the stream after set.seed(5), so they depend on chunk order. The conditional-clone, copula-shape, grain and events fixtures reseed with set.seed(42), set.seed(7), set.seed(3) and set.seed(5), so each of those sections runs on its own. Every mask(), mask_set() and jitter_coordinates() call also passes seed = 1L. Package versions follow.
